newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Milosevic concedes opposition vote win in Nis. [CORRECTED 20:50 GMT]
newsitem.headline: Milosevic concedes opposition vote win in Nis. [CORRECTED 20:50 GMT]

text.p: President Slobodan Milosevic, in a big concession to pro-democracy protesters, admitted on Wednesday that an opposition coalition won recent municipal elections in Serbia's second largest city, Nis.

His Socialist (SPS) government also promised to rectify "every irregularity" in connection with its decision to annul opposition election victories in 15 Serbian cities including Nis and the capital, Belgrade.
In acknowledging their loss in Nis, the Socialists wavered seriously for the first time in a marathon battle of wills with the opposition over the outcome of the voting.

Cancellation of the November 17 election results triggered a wave of street protests, now in their eighth straight week, shaking the foundations of leftist rule in Serbian-led Yugoslavia dating to 1945.

The official news agency Tanjug said the Serbian government agreed that Zajedno had won Nis after a Justice Ministry inquiry ordered by Milosevic late last month after he met protesting students from the southern city.

"On the basis of documents inspected by the Justice Ministry, the Zajedno political organisation won 37 seats, the Socialist Party of Serbia 32 and the Serbian Radical Party one seat in Nis local council," Tanjug said.

"The government expects the (SPS-dominated) municipal electoral commission in Nis...to recognise this indubitable fact, withdraw its earlier decision on repeating local elections in 17 Nis districts and establish the final results of the elections, thereby creating the necessary conditions for forming a new local council in Nis," it said.

Zajedno said it won 41 seats in the Nis council and has demanded that its election victories, verified by a visiting Organisation for Security and Cooperation In Europe (OSCE) team, be reinstated in full in exchange for ending its protests.
Hearing of Tanjug's report, Zajedno said the government's decision was a "confirmation of the correctness of the Nis court ruling 15 or so days ago".
That court ordered Zajedno's victory restored, but the municipal election commission disregarded the directive and decided to rerun the voting in 17 wards.

Zajedno's legal spokeswoman, Vesna Rakic-Vodinelic, was quoted by independent news agency Beta as saying it remained to be seen whether the Nis electoral commission would heed the central government's decision.
Zoran Djindjic, a Zajedno leader, told Reuters the opposition coalition would contest the government's finding that it won 37 (corrects from 32), not 41 seats, in Nis.
"We will not be satisfied and will continue our protests until all the November 17 election results are recognised and until the media and judiciary are freed in Serbia," he said.

Tanjug said that, aside from Nis, "the government would like to make clear that every (election) irregularity established, regardless of protests, will be rectified in keeping with the law and within legal institutions".
Milosevic's government had responded to the OSCE inquiry last week by admitting Zajedno had prevailed in nine wards of Belgrade and three smaller provincial cities.
But the Socialists said nothing about Belgrade's policy-making municipal assembly and contended that, in the other cities, no party won a majority or that the results required further examination.
The SPS had cited unspecified "irregularities" as its reason for invalidating the November 17 election.
